proposal: The chapter recommends that the United States end its funding of and withdraw from the OECD, withdraw from the IMF and the World Bank and end its contributions, and reject OECD-led efforts to coordinate a global minimum corporate tax, which it describes as a tax cartel. status_summary: The global-tax strand has moved: a 2025-01-20 presidential memorandum directed Treasury to tell the OECD that prior global tax deal commitments have no force in the United States without Congress, and on 2026-01-05 Treasury announced a side-by-side agreement with the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework under which U.S.-headquartered companies are exempt from Pillar Two and remain subject only to U.S. minimum taxes. The withdrawal strand has not: Executive Order 14199 (2025-02-04) ordered a 180-day review of international organizations, and the 2026-01-07 memorandum withdrawing the United States from 66 organizations does not list the OECD, IMF or World Bank and says review of further findings remains ongoing. Treasury's undated FY 2027 international programs budget summary shows no IBRD funding in FY 2026 or FY 2027 because the FY 2025 payment completed U.S. share purchases under the 2018 capital increase, $1.07 billion enacted for the World Bank's IDA affiliate in FY 2026 and $866.7 million requested for FY 2027, and a request for an IMF quota increase with a smaller New Arrangements to Borrow commitment; it proposes no withdrawal. Treasury Secretary Bessent's statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee of 2026-04-15 says the United States is committed to a strong, quota-based and adequately resourced IMF and to securing congressional approval for the 16th General Review of Quotas, and calls for the World Bank to keep to its core mission; it does not mention withdrawal. A Center for Global Development analysis published in September 2025 reported no FY 2025 obligations to the OECD in the data then available and no OECD funding in the FY 2026 request for the State Department's international organizations account; the enacted OECD level was not found.

timeline.event: Presidential memorandum on the OECD global tax deal directs Treasury and the U.S. representative to the OECD to notify the OECD that prior commitments have no force in the United States absent congressional enactment, and directs Treasury to review foreign tax practices and report within 60 days.

Executive Order 14199 orders a 180-day review of international organizations, conventions and treaties for possible withdrawal; international financial institutions are not mentioned (90 FR 9275, published 2025-02-10).
Treasury announces a side-by-side agreement with the OECD/G20 Inclusive Framework exempting U.S.-headquartered companies from Pillar Two while keeping them subject to U.S. global minimum taxes.

Presidential memorandum directs withdrawal from 66 organizations (35 non-UN and 31 UN); its list includes no international financial institution and does not name the OECD, IMF or World Bank, and it states that review of further State Department findings remains ongoing (91 FR 2281, published 2026-01-16).

title: Withdraw from the OECD, IMF and World Bank and resist the global minimum tax
uncertainties: The conclusion that no withdrawal from the OECD, IMF or World Bank has occurred rests on the 66-organization list, the FY2027 Treasury budget document (which proposes no withdrawal and does not mention the OECD) and secondary reporting; no administration statement was found announcing a decision on those three bodies, and the result of the 180-day review ordered in February 2025 was not located. The OECD funding picture comes from a think-tank blog and a Bloomberg Tax article about proposals; the enacted OECD amount and any actual FY2026 payment were not found. The Treasury budget document, titled an executive summary, shows no publication date and its source entry is marked undated; Secretary Bessent's position rests on his written Treasury statement to the International Monetary and Financial Committee of 2026-04-15; no transcript of oral remarks was checked. The tax-assistance protocol and account-exchange agreement were not checked. Update 2026-10-15: the House Appropriations Committee release on its FY2027 national security and State bill (2026-04-22) names neither the IMF, IDA nor the OECD, but says the bill eliminates contributions to unnamed multilateral organizations and requires opposition to MDB lending to China. A wire report dated 2026-10-10 said the Treasury Secretary would skip the October 2026 IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, with a deputy-led delegation focused on imbalances and sovereign debt transparency, and mentioned no withdrawal. Searches found no 2026 Inclusive Framework decision beyond the January side-by-side package. The 2026-01-07 memorandum states that the President's review of further State Department findings remains ongoing, so a later withdrawal decision cannot be excluded. Reports from Bloomberg Tax and the Center for Global Development are kept as context rather than timeline actions. The stage rests on the operative global-tax strand; the withdrawal strand has no operative action, so progress sits at the bottom of the in_progress band.
